analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a quality niche play on India's petrochemical and energy capex supercycle, with impressive 24.5% revenue CAGR and 22.4% net profit CAGR over five years. However, at 34.8x P/E with promoter holding below 50% and a concerning FY2025 cash flow collapse, the current price already reflects significant optimism.
key_strengths: Structural tailwinds: process equipment demand driven by India's petrochemical, LNG, hydrogen, and refinery capex boom — 10+ year runway
Consistent financial execution: revenue INR 245→733 Cr, net profit INR 43→118 Cr over five years; operating margins stable at ~17.9%
Clean balance sheet: D/E at 0.25 despite capacity expansion; 62-year operating track record signals durability
key_risks: Cash flow deterioration: FY2025 OCF turned negative (-7 Cr) vs INR 118 Cr net profit — severe working capital strain signals execution risk on large orders
Valuation premium: 34.8x P/E and 6.36x P/B are rich for a cyclical capital equipment business dependent on lumpy orders; leaves little margin of safety
Promoter holding at only 40.92% — below my 50% threshold — raises governance alignment concerns; low skin-in-the-game for minority shareholders
red_flags: FY2025 free cash flow of -51 Cr despite INR 118 Cr net profit — profit-to-cash conversion has broken down
Borrowings surged from near-zero to INR 158 Cr in FY2025 — company is funding working capital with debt as order book scales
Promoter stake at 40.92% is sub-50% — in India, this signals weaker alignment with minority shareholders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Anup Engineering is a genuinely interesting India industrial story — a 62-year-old Ahmedabad-based fabricator of specialty process equipment (heat exchangers, pressure vessels, reactors) riding the structural capex boom in India's oil, gas, petrochemical, and LNG sectors. Revenue growth of 24.5% CAGR and net profit growth of 22.4% CAGR over FY2020–25 is impressive, and operating margins holding at 17.9% demonstrate pricing power and execution quality. The recently completed capacity expansion (CWIP peaked at INR 87 Cr in FY2023, now normalized to 15 Cr) positions the company to handle a larger order book — exactly the kind of forward-thinking capex I like to see from management.

However, FY2025 raises serious questions. Despite reporting INR 118 Cr net profit, operating cash flow was -7 Cr and FCF was -51 Cr — a massive divergence. This signals working capital has ballooned, likely from large orders with unfavorable milestone billing terms. Simultaneously, borrowings jumped to INR 158 Cr, meaning the company is now borrowing to fund day-to-day operations. This is forgivable if it reflects order book buildup, but it must reverse in FY2026 or it becomes a structural concern. At 34.8x P/E, the market is pricing perfection into a cyclical, lumpy-order business — that is not how I like to buy. I would revisit at 24-26x P/E if FCF normalizes.
